kicker: FOR NYC FIRMS RENOVATING HIGH-END HOMES
title: Turn the site visit into a renovation quote that sells the design.
description: A custom quote generator for premium NYC renovation firms: room-by-room scope, your approved pricing and interior design concepts in one client-ready proposal.
lead: Your client wants to see the home they could have—and understand what it will cost. We build a quote generator that brings the site notes, room-by-room scope, material selections and interior design concept into one branded proposal. Your estimator checks the numbers. Your designer checks the vision. Your sales team gets a clearer next conversation.
audience: Owner-led NYC renovation and design-build firms serving high-end apartment, brownstone and townhouse clients.
Owners and heads of preconstruction whose estimators and interior designers build each proposal together.
Teams with qualified enquiries, several projects in progress and repeatable pricing or past estimates to work from.

problems.title: The designer and estimator rebuild the same brief
problems.body: Site photographs, measurements, client preferences and meeting notes arrive in different places. We turn the approved inputs into a shared room-by-room brief with missing decisions clearly marked.

problems.title: The price and the interior concept tell different stories
problems.body: A beautiful mood board can omit the cost implications; an estimate can fail to explain the design. We connect the selected finishes, scope lines and concept pages in one proposal.

problems.title: Every client change creates another round of document work
problems.body: A different vanity, stone or cabinetry option can affect the allowance and several pages. The workflow prepares a revised version and highlights the changes for the designer and estimator.

deliverables.title: A quote generator using your commercial rules
deliverables.body: Draft line items from your approved scope library, rate card and allowances. Apply the calculation rules you approve and surface missing rates, uncertain quantities and items requiring a supplier quote.

deliverables.title: Interior design embedded in the proposal
deliverables.body: Room concept pages, material palettes, reference imagery and selected options alongside the relevant work. Any generated visual is labeled as a concept and checked by your designer before the client sees it.

deliverables.title: A proposal built for a decision
deliverables.body: A branded PDF with room-by-room scope, the reviewed price, options, allowances, exclusions and next steps. The homeowner can see the proposed result and the decisions needed to move forward.

deliverables.title: A controlled handoff into the project
deliverables.body: Retain the approved selections, quote version and unresolved items for the design and delivery team. Construction Set preparation and material schedules can follow as a separately agreed next stage.

workflow.title: Capture the renovation brief
workflow.body: Bring together the approved site notes, photographs, plans, client preferences and room list. Ask for missing measurements or choices instead of inventing them.

workflow.title: Build scope, design and price together
workflow.body: Prepare the room scope and concept pages, then match priced items to your approved rates and allowances. Keep optional upgrades separate from the base proposal.

workflow.title: Review the commercial and design details
workflow.body: The estimator checks quantities, supplier inputs and pricing. The designer reviews selections and visual concepts. Both can request a controlled revision.

workflow.title: Present the approved proposal
workflow.body: An authorized person approves release. Keep the final scope and design decisions available for the next sales conversation and project handoff.

example.title: One Manhattan kitchen. Two design options. One clear quote.
example.body: After a site visit, the client is choosing between painted cabinetry and a natural oak upgrade. Today the designer builds a concept deck while the estimator works in a separate file. The proposed workflow assembles both options in one package, carries the approved price difference into the quote and flags an appliance specification still needed. Your team reviews it before the client receives it.

example.output: A branded proposal with base scope, priced upgrade, interior concept pages, material selections and a short list of open decisions.
example.reviewer: Your estimator approves the commercial details, your designer approves the concept, and your owner or sales lead authorizes release.

systems.body: Keep the project folders, estimating files and design tools your team already uses. We connect the specific inputs needed for the first quote type and return the proposal in your format.

Interior design references and selection libraries

pilot.body: Pick one repeatable project type, such as a kitchen or bathroom renovation. We compare the original brief, estimate and presentation, define the rules that made them correct, then build a quote-and-design pilot around those examples.

faqs.q: Will the generator decide our prices?
faqs.a: Your firm owns the pricing. The workflow uses the rates, quantities, allowances and calculation rules you approve. Missing supplier costs and uncertain quantities remain visible for the estimator to resolve.

faqs.q: Can the interior design be part of the quote itself?
faqs.a: Yes. The offer includes agreed concept pages, selected finishes and design options within the branded proposal. The designer controls the aesthetic direction and approves any generated imagery. Detailed drawings and technical documentation are separate deliverables.

faqs.q: How quickly could we issue a quote?
faqs.a: We measure that on your project type. The related 29-minute demonstration was one design-document run, not a complete priced renovation quote. In the pilot we record generation time, estimator time, designer time and the final approval delay so you can assess the actual sales turnaround.

cta.title: Bring your last renovation quote. Let’s improve the next one.

kicker: FOR U.S. CPA, CAS, BOOKKEEPING AND PAYROLL FIRMS
title: Get client work ready for the accountant sooner.
description: Connect missing-document checks, payroll inputs and client follow-ups so your accounting team can move recurring work toward professional review.
lead: A monthly package is almost complete. One recurring invoice is missing, a statement belongs to the wrong period and payroll is waiting on an approved input. We build a shared work queue that spots those gaps, prepares the next request and gives each exception an owner. Your team spends its attention on the work that needs judgment.
audience: Established U.S. CPA and client accounting services firms handling recurring bookkeeping and payroll for business clients.
Managing partners and operations managers whose coordinators check the same client packages every month.
Practices where email, client portals, accounting software and payroll systems each hold part of the status.

problems.title: A missing item can look like a finished package
problems.body: A document may be present but belong to another month, or a recurring invoice may have stopped arriving. We check the agreed client checklist and permitted history, then flag the difference with its source.

problems.title: The same client gets checked by several people
problems.body: A coordinator searches email, a bookkeeper checks a folder and an operations manager asks for status. A shared view shows the latest check, the open question and who owns it.

problems.title: The deadline arrives before the missing information
problems.body: When the team discovers a gap late, professional work pauses. Preparing earlier, specific follow-ups can give the client a clearer request and the team a visible escalation path.

deliverables.title: A client-and-period readiness view
deliverables.body: An agreed checklist showing received, missing and review-needed items for one monthly service. Link the status back to the relevant source and show when it was last checked.

deliverables.title: Recurring invoice and document gap detection
deliverables.body: Flag expected items absent from the current package, using your approved rules and historical patterns. A missing recurring item is a question for review, not a conclusion that a transaction occurred.

deliverables.title: Payroll preparation and an exception queue
deliverables.body: Assemble the required payroll inputs and show completeness issues with an owner. Keep uncertain matches, conflicting information and missing approvals separate from ready work.

deliverables.title: Specific follow-ups ready to approve
deliverables.body: Draft a request naming the client, period and outstanding item. Your team checks the recipient and wording, then records the action in the agreed practice workflow.

workflow.title: Choose a recurring service cycle
workflow.body: Define one bookkeeping or payroll package, its expected inputs and the team member who decides when it is ready.

workflow.title: Match and check the incoming material
workflow.body: Propose the client, period and document type. Compare against the checklist and agreed recurring patterns; uncertain matches go to review.

workflow.title: Prepare the next useful action
workflow.body: Draft the missing-item request or internal task, with its source, owner and due date. Keep a late client response distinct from an internal processing issue.

workflow.title: Approve and hand off ready work
workflow.body: The coordinator approves follow-ups and resolves matches. The accountant or payroll specialist receives the checked package and remains responsible for professional decisions.

example.label: ILLUSTRATIVE SERVICE CYCLE — NOT A CUSTOMER RESULT
example.title: A recurring vendor invoice is missing. Payroll has one open input.
example.body: A business client normally supplies a monthly equipment-maintenance invoice. This month it is absent, and the payroll package is also awaiting an approved timesheet. Instead of two staff members searching the same inbox, the workflow prepares two specific exceptions and a consolidated request. The coordinator verifies whether the invoice is actually expected and approves the follow-up.
example.input: The client checklist, current-period documents, permitted invoice history, payroll requirements and the responsible staff member.
example.output: A readiness view, two clearly owned exceptions and a draft client request identifying exactly what is needed.
example.reviewer: The coordinator approves the request; qualified accounting and payroll staff review the resulting work package.

systems.body: Your practice, accounting and payroll systems keep their existing roles. We connect the status and documents required for the selected service cycle, including freshness and connection failures.
systems.footnote: Specific integrations depend on APIs, subscriptions and permissions. Financial changes, payroll submission and tax decisions remain subject to your professional controls and explicit approval.

pilot.title: Prove it on one monthly client group.
pilot.body: Choose a recurring process and a manageable group of clients. Compare the current checking and chasing effort with the reviewed pilot, including missing, duplicate, late and ambiguous documents.
includes: Map one monthly service and its handoffs
Agree client matching and expected-document rules
Build readiness, exception and follow-up views

measures: Staff minutes spent checking and chasing per client
Time until the package is ready for professional review
Correct client, period and document matches
Age of unresolved exceptions and repeat client requests

faqs.q: Our software already sends reminders. What does this add?
faqs.a: The useful gap is often deciding what to request. We assess whether your existing tools can match an attachment to the right client and month, detect an expected item that is absent and show an owner for the exception. Native features may already solve part of the problem.

faqs.q: Does it calculate or submit payroll?
faqs.a: This offer prepares a complete, reviewable package and surfaces missing information. Payroll calculations, changes and submission stay with authorized people and your existing controls. Any additional action requires its own defined scope.

faqs.q: How do we know it creates capacity?
faqs.a: Measure checking time, chasing time and review time separately before and during the pilot. Also track incorrect matches and repeated requests. Faster preparation is useful only if the professional receives a package they can trust.

kicker: FOR U.S. REAL ESTATE TRANSACTION COUNSEL
title: Spend review time on the property issue. Have the evidence ready.
description: Prepare a source-linked property due-diligence report that helps real estate counsel review document conflicts and client questions more efficiently.
lead: The purchase is moving, but the document package still needs a careful comparison: unit details, plans, recorded attachments and the provisions that affect the buyer. We build a workflow that assembles those facts, flags discrepancies and puts the relevant page beside each finding. Your attorney can move from searching files to reviewing the issue.
audience: U.S. boutique and midsize real estate law firms advising buyers or investors on repeated property acquisitions.
Real estate practice partners and senior paralegals who repeatedly compare similar condo or property document packages.
Teams with one defined jurisdiction, a repeatable transaction type and a qualified reviewer who owns the checklist.

problems.title: The same fact appears in several places
problems.body: A unit description, parking reference or attachment may be recorded in different documents and formats. The workflow locates the agreed fields and presents the sources together.

problems.title: The evidence is harder to find than the summary
problems.body: A reviewer needs more than a confident paragraph. Every material draft finding is paired with the document, page and relevant excerpt or image crop needed to check it.

problems.title: Missing evidence becomes a last-minute question
problems.body: An absent page or unclear scan can block a conclusion. The workflow identifies what cannot be established and keeps it visible in the matter’s open-item list.

deliverables.title: A matter-specific comparison checklist
deliverables.body: Your qualified reviewer defines the jurisdiction, eligible document package, fields to compare and questions that belong in the first version.

deliverables.title: A draft diligence report with evidence
deliverables.body: A comparison table and findings with source references, pages and relevant excerpts or crops. Clearly distinguish supported matches, potential discrepancies and items not determined.

deliverables.title: A discrepancy and request list
deliverables.body: A concise list of conflicting facts, missing documents and questions for the attorney to assess. Prepare follow-up wording only after the responsible reviewer decides what to request.

deliverables.title: An approved client-summary format
deliverables.body: Turn the reviewed findings into the concise format your firm uses to explain the matter to its client. The attorney edits and approves the summary before release.

workflow.title: Check that the matter is eligible
workflow.body: Confirm the transaction type and jurisdiction, then verify the approved document set is complete and readable enough for the agreed checks.

workflow.title: Locate the facts and their counterparts
workflow.body: Extract the specified identifiers, descriptions and attachments. Find the relevant passages or plan areas in the other approved sources.

workflow.title: Prepare the evidence and open questions
workflow.body: Assemble the comparison report, preserve conflicting sources and flag anything the supplied documents cannot establish.

workflow.title: Review and explain the result
workflow.body: The attorney evaluates significance, corrects the draft and approves any requests or client summary. The system does not clear the transaction.

example.label: ILLUSTRATIVE U.S. ADAPTATION — NOT A CUSTOMER RESULT
example.title: The parking reference does not line up across the file.
example.body: A buyer’s counsel reviews a condominium package using a locally approved checklist. A parking reference in one document differs from the corresponding exhibit. The workflow places both sources in the draft report and flags an unclear amendment. The attorney checks the evidence, determines whether the difference matters and decides which clarification to request.
example.input: The attorney-selected transaction documents, relevant plans and exhibits, and the jurisdiction-specific comparison checklist.
example.output: A source-linked comparison, the conflicting parking references, the unresolved amendment question and a draft matter summary.
example.reviewer: The responsible real estate attorney interprets the documents, decides the legal significance and approves client-facing work.

systems.body: Use the matter folders and document-management process your firm approves. We define where the source files are read, where drafts are stored and which team members can review them.
items: Firm diligence checklists and report templates
systems.footnote: The initial offer uses documents your team selects. Public-record retrieval and additional jurisdictions require separate validation. Legal opinions and transaction decisions remain with the responsible professionals.

pilot.title: Benchmark one transaction type with your attorney.
pilot.body: Use completed matters from one jurisdiction to define the expected findings and evidence. Include unclear scans, missing pages and real discrepancies. The goal is a draft the reviewer can check efficiently, with important uncertainty still visible.

Define the checklist and material error categories

measures: Preparation plus attorney-review minutes per eligible matter
Critical omissions, unsupported findings and corrections
Time from complete package to an approved client summary

faqs.q: Can you reuse the same workflow across states?
faqs.a: The review pattern can transfer, but the document requirements and legal logic need local validation. Start with one jurisdiction and transaction type. Additional jurisdictions enter the scope after your qualified reviewer defines and tests the relevant checks.

faqs.q: What if a source is missing or the plan is unclear?
faqs.a: The affected finding stays unresolved. The draft identifies the missing or unreadable evidence so the reviewer can request a better source or handle the point manually.

faqs.q: Does a fast draft mean the transaction is cleared?
faqs.a: No. Draft preparation and legal approval are separate steps. The attorney determines what the documents mean and whether further work is required. Pilot timing includes the effort needed to review and correct the draft.

Firms with a working ATS or CRM, several consultants and valuable account history spread across records, email and meeting notes.

problems.title: The opportunity is buried in an old conversation
problems.body: A timing signal or hiring priority may be recorded in a note that the account owner has not reopened. Bring the relevant history forward with its source and date so the consultant can judge whether it still applies.

problems.title: Partners prepare from a blank page
problems.body: Meeting preparation often means searching the CRM, asking colleagues and scanning email. A consistent brief gathers the agreed account context and makes unanswered questions explicit.

problems.title: Good intentions never become an owned next step
problems.body: A promised introduction or post-meeting follow-up can disappear between people. The workflow proposes an owner and next action, then records the consultant’s decision.

deliverables.title: A weekly client-opportunity queue
deliverables.body: Account actions suggested from your approved rules, such as an agreed check-in date or open commitment. Each item includes the reason, relevant source and proposed consultant owner.

deliverables.title: A partner-ready client brief
deliverables.body: A concise account view covering prior assignments, relevant contacts, client priorities, recent conversations and questions to confirm. Show source links and dates so the consultant can check freshness.

deliverables.title: A thoughtful follow-up draft
deliverables.body: Prepare a short message or call outline tied to the actual relationship. The account owner edits the content, decides whether contact is appropriate and controls sending.

deliverables.title: An opportunity and handoff record
deliverables.body: Capture the approved next step, its owner and the meeting outcome in the agreed CRM workflow. Keep context available when another consultant joins the account.

workflow.title: Select the client accounts and source rules
workflow.body: Start with a defined account group and the CRM, meeting notes and business communications your firm permits the workflow to use.

workflow.title: Find the relevant commitment or signal
workflow.body: Apply the follow-up rules your partners approve. Preserve the original source and date, and flag uncertain contact matches or stale context.

workflow.title: Prepare the business conversation
workflow.body: Assemble the client brief, questions to confirm and a proposed next action. Draft the outreach only when the supporting relationship context is available.

workflow.title: Let the partner choose and follow through
workflow.body: The account owner approves, edits or dismisses the suggestion. Record the actual next step and outcome so future preparation reflects what happened.
